newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico stock gains boosted by Wall Street recovery.
newsitem.headline: Mexico stock gains boosted by Wall Street recovery.

text.p: Mexican stocks enhanced midday gains following a late recovery on Wall Street after zizagging through a thin-volume session as caution on volatile U.S. markets alternated with strong domestic fundamentals, traders and analyst said.
"A very strange day on Wall Street, but it ended up so we did too. But fundamentally the bourse is very strong. That's why we fended off falling prices in New York," a Mexico City desk trader said.
The leading IPC share index ended up 11.17 points, or 0.30 percent, at 3,752.47.
Volume was slow at 55.8 million shares traded.
The Dow Jones ended up 48.72 points at 6,526.07. But analysts in Mexico noted the bourse was in positive territory even when the Dow had reached a low of 6,404.84 points.

"We are optimistic, we are decoupling ourselves from New York, Mexico's fundamentals are good. Furthermore, the market is cheap, but you need to tread carefully when picking stocks because growth is not even," an equity analyst said.
"Volume shows few foreigners were in the bourse, they prefer other emerging markets," he added.
Telmex L, which accounted for one quarter of all shares traded in Mexico, weighed most heavily on the bourse and ended down two centavos at 15.64 pesos. Its ADRs closed up 1/8 at 39-1/8.
Dealers said a stronger peso encouraged arbitrage trading, whereby brokers sold L shares in Mexico to buy ADRs in New York.
News the U.S. Department of Commerce had decided to raise anti-dumping tariffs on Mexican cement exports led to a volatile session for the three cement makers included in the IPC index.
Cemex B shares ended up 25 centavos at 31.95, while its CPO series gained 40 centavos to 29.00 pesos. The B and CPO series were the third- and fourth-most traded stocks of the session.
Apasco meanwhile gained two pesos to 54.80 pesos.
Analysts noted the tariffs would hit neither company hard, as Cemex had a diversified export base, and Apasco exported little to the U.S. market.
Traders noted Smith Barney had also initiated coverage of both stocks with a buy recommendation in early trade.

Analysts said the anti-dumping measures would, however, hurt Grupo Cementos de Chihuahua (GCC), a cement maker in norhtern Mexico which depends heavily on exports to the U.S. market. GCC ended down six centavos at 7.90 pesos.
"GCC took the bad news very well, considering the expected downside potential," a trader said.
Analysts also drew attention to strong gains posted by holding company Femsa and conglomerate Desc.
Femsa rose 85 centavos to 36.20 pesos, and Desc climbed 70 centavos to 54.00 pesos.

"Femsa gained on forthcoming price increases on soft drinks... Desc was bolstered by its investments in exports and manufacturing, particularly auto parts which are selling well, and a recovery in domestic consumption is also helping," an analyst said.
((-- Mexico City newsroom +525 728-7907))
